items.question: An access review at a supermarket chain found that the `search_documents` tool on its internal MCP server runs under a credential with read access to the whole document store, including HR case files. No one has retrieved an HR file through the agent, but nothing prevents it. The tool's actual job is searching store operating procedures. What should the team do next?

options.A: Add an output filter that redacts HR case-file content from `search_documents` results.
options.B: Narrow the tool description so the model does not reach for it on HR-related questions.
options.C: Reissue the credential scoped to operating procedures, then re-run the access review.
options.D: Require human approval on every `search_documents` call until the scope can be reduced.

items.question: What does each additional tool declared in a request cost, beyond the work of maintaining it?

options.A: An extra round trip per turn, since the model evaluates each declared tool in sequence.
options.B: Prefix space on every turn, plus one more candidate the model must discriminate between.
options.C: Nothing after the first request of a conversation, since definitions are sent only once.
options.D: Additional output tokens, because the model reasons about each declared tool before answering.

items.question: A wealth manager's advisory agent has grown to seventy tools and selection accuracy has fallen. A senior engineer proposes merging them into eight dispatcher tools, each taking an `operation` enum and an operation-specific payload, to bring the advertised count down. How should the architect respond?

options.A: Adopt it; fewer advertised tools reliably improves selection accuracy and prefix cost.
options.B: Adopt it for the read-only tools and leave the write tools individually addressable.
options.C: Adopt it and add strict schemas so malformed operation payloads are caught at generation.
options.D: Reject it; cut the tools visible per request instead of hiding seventy behind eight.

items.question: Which TWO statements accurately describe the cost of declaring a large number of tools on every request? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Each declared tool adds a round trip to the turn, whether or not it is used.
options.B: Every tool's schema occupies the request prefix on every turn, used or not.
options.C: Definitions for tools the model does not call are omitted from the request by the API.
options.D: Selection accuracy degrades as the set accumulates tools with overlapping purposes.
options.E: Output token usage scales with the number of tools declared on the request.

items.question: An engineering conglomerate wants one internal assistant to reach roughly nine hundred tools spanning procurement, HSE, maintenance and finance. Any given conversation touches a handful. Sessions are long and the team relies on prefix caching for affordability. Declaring everything is far beyond the budget. What architecture should they adopt?

options.A: Keep a small always-loaded core plus a discovery mechanism that appends the schemas the model asks for.
options.B: Predict the likely subset each turn and rewrite the tools array to match before every request.
options.C: Split into a dozen assistants, each with a fixed set, and have users pick the right one.
options.D: Publish all nine hundred schemas as a document the assistant reads through a single fetch tool.

items.question: A B2B software vendor's support agent covers five product lines, each with about twelve tools. Tickets arrive tagged with the product line, and cross-product questions are rare. All sixty tools are currently declared on every request, and the agent sometimes calls a tool from the wrong product. What is the most appropriate change?

options.A: Keep all sixty declared and disambiguate by prefixing every tool name with its product line.
options.B: Attach only the tools for the ticket's product line, selected in the application before the request.
options.C: Add a `choose_product_line` tool the model calls first, then have it work within that line.
options.D: Put a routing table in the system prompt mapping symptoms to the correct product's tools.

items.question: In a design where most tool definitions are deferred and loaded only when the model asks for them, what must always remain loaded?

options.A: Nothing; the model can request any tool by name from an empty starting set.
options.B: Every read-only tool, so the model always has a safe default action.
options.C: The tools most frequently used across recent production traffic.
options.D: The discovery mechanism itself, plus at least one tool the model can act with.

items.question: A charity's grants assistant declares twelve tools. Six months of traces show four of them have never been called, and their capabilities are covered by other tools. What should the team do?

options.A: Remove them; unused definitions cost prefix space and add candidates to every selection.
options.B: Keep them; a tool that is never called costs nothing at runtime or in the prefix.
options.C: Keep them but mark them deprecated in their descriptions so the model deprioritises them.
options.D: Merge them into one tool so the advertised count falls without losing the capability.

items.question: A team is deciding whether to introduce dynamic tool discovery instead of declaring their full set up front. Which TWO conditions argue against it? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: The set is small and stable, so a fixed prefix caches well and discovery adds a hop.
options.B: The organisation maintains more than twenty tools in total across its systems.
options.C: All the tools in the set are read-only lookups with no side effects.
options.D: The team has moved to a higher-capability model tier for this agent.
options.E: Nearly every request needs the same handful of tools from the catalogue.

items.question: A hotel group's operations assistant uses discovery over a catalogue of roughly four hundred tools. Guest-recovery workflows fail because the assistant never finds `issue_service_recovery_credit`; its description reads "Creates a compensatory ledger entry against a reservation", while staff and the model both search using words like refund, goodwill and compensation. The team's proposal is to load all four hundred tools whenever discovery returns nothing. What should they do next?

options.A: Increase the number of candidate tools discovery returns per search from five to twenty.
options.B: Treat discovery as retrieval: rewrite descriptions in users' vocabulary and measure recall.
options.C: Adopt the team's fallback and load all four hundred tools when a search comes back empty.
options.D: Instruct the assistant to rephrase and retry its search up to three times before it gives up.

items.question: A media measurement company exposes an MCP server to partner agencies. Each partner's access token carries scopes reflecting what they bought — some have panel data only, some also have cross-platform attribution. Which TWO practices should the server follow? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Advertise the complete tool list and rely on the model to avoid tools the partner has not bought.
options.B: Have the partner pass their entitlement tier as a tool argument that the handler checks.
options.C: Filter the advertised tool list by the scopes in the verified token, so unavailable capabilities are never offered.
options.D: Re-check the scope at execution, because advertising a narrower list is not authorisation.
options.E: Issue one long-lived shared token per partner organisation so scope checks stay simple.

items.question: A non-streaming response returns with `stop_reason` set to `max_tokens`. What has the calling application just been told?

options.A: The request's input exceeded the context window, so no assistant content was produced.
options.B: Generation stopped at the output cap, so the returned content is incomplete.
options.C: The model finished its answer normally and the token count happened to land just under the cap.
options.D: One of the request's configured stop sequences matched and generation was cut at that point.

items.question: A legal technology firm answers questions against a fixed 40,000-token bundle of clause precedents and an invariant answering policy. The engineer building the prompt places the user's question first — reasoning that the model should know what it is looking for before it reads — then the policy, then the precedent bundle, with a cache breakpoint at the very end. After a month, the cache hit rate is effectively zero and cost per query is above the pre-caching baseline. Traffic is steady at several hundred queries an hour.

options.A: Place a second cache breakpoint immediately after the user's question so the question segment is also cached.
options.B: Raise `max_tokens` so the model has headroom to work through all 40,000 tokens of precedent in one pass.
options.C: Reorder the request so the policy and precedent bundle come first with the breakpoint at their end, and the question last.
options.D: Move the workload to the Batch API so the bundle's cost is amortised across the day's several hundred queries.

items.question: A food-delivery platform runs 60 stateless workers that each call Claude to summarise restaurant reviews. All workers were deployed from the same image and share a retry helper that reissues a failed call immediately, up to ten times. During the evening peak the account begins returning rate-limit responses; the workers all retry in lockstep, the rate-limit rate climbs rather than settling, and effective throughput has fallen below what the account's published limit should support. What should the team do next?

options.A: Replace immediate retry with exponential backoff plus randomised jitter, and honour retry-after guidance.
options.B: Raise the HTTP client timeout so in-flight requests have longer to complete before the retry helper fires.
options.C: Scale the fleet from 60 to 100 workers so the review backlog drains faster once the limit window clears.
options.D: Fail each rate-limited call over to a smaller, cheaper model tier and reissue it there without delay.

items.question: An architect is auditing why a prompt-cache hit rate collapsed after a release. Which TWO of the following invalidate the cached prefix for subsequent requests? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Appending a new user message after the final cache breakpoint on the next turn.
options.B: Editing one sentence of the system prompt that sits before the cache breakpoint.
options.C: Raising `max_tokens` on the request while leaving all message and tool content unchanged.
options.D: Adding a new tool definition to the tool list the request sends alongside the prompt.
options.E: Issuing the request from a different application server belonging to the same organisation.

items.question: A streaming-media company re-describes roughly two million newly ingested catalogue assets each night, with results needed before the 06:00 catalogue build. During the day, editors request on-demand descriptions and expect them in a couple of seconds. Both workloads go through the same realtime endpoint. The nightly job now regularly overruns into the business day, saturates the account's throughput ceiling, and pushes editor latency from two seconds to over thirty.

options.A: Move both workloads to the Batch API and have the editor tool poll for each description as it completes.
options.B: Keep both on the realtime endpoint and give editor requests a higher-priority client-side queue.
options.C: Split the nightly job across several additional API keys in the same organisation to draw on more headroom.
options.D: Move the nightly enrichment to the Batch API and leave editor requests on the realtime endpoint.

items.question: A manufacturing group generates long root-cause reports from equipment telemetry; outputs routinely run several thousand tokens and engineers need them during shift handover, within a few minutes of asking. The HTTP client uses the platform team's house default of a 30-second timeout with two retries. Server-side measurement shows p99 generation latency for this call is near 70 seconds. Since launch, about 8% of report requests time out, retry, and time out again. The API bill has risen while the completion rate has fallen.

options.A: Keep the 30-second timeout and raise the retry count to five, so one attempt eventually completes inside the window.
options.B: Size this endpoint's timeout from its measured latency, and stream so the deadline applies to first-token latency.
options.C: Cap `max_tokens` low enough that generation reliably finishes inside the 30-second window, accepting shorter reports.
options.D: Move report generation to the Batch API and deliver finished reports into the shift-handover channel asynchronously.

items.question: In a request that uses prompt caching, what does a cache breakpoint designate?

options.A: The point beyond which the model stops reading the context supplied in the request.
options.B: The end of a prefix that is eligible for caching, covering everything ahead of it.
options.C: An isolated block that is cached independently of whatever precedes it in the request.
options.D: The boundary at which older conversation turns are summarised into a digest and dropped.

items.question: A telco is replacing the blocking call behind its support widget with a streamed one so agents see text as it is produced. The widget renders into a live transcript pane and the conversation is persisted afterwards. Which TWO behaviours must the client implement for this integration to be correct? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Parse each delta as a self-contained JSON document, then render that fragment into the transcript pane before the next arrives.
options.B: Accumulate the deltas in arrival order and treat the text as final only once the block and message end events arrive.
options.C: Read the response's final output-token usage from the stream's opening event so billing can be recorded up front.
options.D: Disable retries on this endpoint, because a request that has already emitted bytes can never be reissued.
options.E: Handle a failure that arrives after part of the response has already been rendered into the live transcript pane.

items.question: A specialty insurer runs claim triage against a 9,000-token underwriting rubric. To let each regional team tune wording, the platform maintains 38 separate prompt variants; each variant serves roughly 15 requests an hour, unevenly spread. Prompt caching was enabled six weeks ago with a breakpoint at the end of each variant's rubric. Cost per request has risen slightly rather than fallen, and the measured hit rate sits below 20%.

options.A: Add a second cache breakpoint midway through each regional variant so more of each prompt is covered.
options.B: Issue a synthetic keep-alive request per variant on a timer so no variant's entry lapses between real requests.
options.C: Consolidate the 38 variants onto one shared rubric prefix and move the regional wording after the breakpoint.
options.D: Disable caching here and cut the 9,000-token rubric down to the rules each region actually cites.

items.question: A three-person team ships a tutoring product for secondary-school maths. Learners complain that the assistant forgets what they said two questions earlier and re-explains material already covered. The engineer who built the integration assumed the endpoint held the session and sends only the newest learner message plus an internal session identifier on each call. Traffic is modest and cost is not the binding constraint; quality complaints are.

options.A: Keep sending only the newest message, but put the session identifier in the system prompt so the model can look up earlier turns.
options.B: Raise `max_tokens` so each reply has room to restate the earlier working before answering the new question.
options.C: Configure a longer cache lifetime so each learner's earlier turns stay available to the model between calls.
options.D: Send the accumulated message history on every call, with a budget that trims or summarises the oldest turns.

items.question: Which classes of API failure should a production client retry automatically, and how?

options.A: Every non-2xx response, using a fixed one-second delay and a bounded retry budget, so no failure class is missed.
options.B: Server-side 5xx failures only; a rate-limit response should be surfaced to the caller as a fatal error.
options.C: Rate-limit responses and transient overload or server errors, with exponential backoff and jitter; not validation errors.
options.D: Request-validation errors, since re-serialising and resending the payload usually clears the malformed field.

items.question: A travel booking platform uses Claude to decide whether a cancellation qualifies for a fee waiver; the decision is posted to a refund service that moves money. Last week a client timeout fired while a decision call was still in flight. The client retried, the retry returned a waiver, and the refund service posted a second payment — the original call had also completed and posted. Finance found the duplicate three days later. The team must stop this class of defect before the next release.

options.A: Set temperature to 0 so a retried decision returns an identical result and the duplicate can be detected by comparing outputs.
options.B: Make the refund service idempotent on a key derived from the cancellation, so a replayed decision cannot post twice.
options.C: Remove retries from the decision call so any timeout surfaces to the customer as a failed cancellation request.
options.D: Extend the client timeout past the observed p99 for the decision call so timeouts stop firing on in-flight work.

items.question: A fashion retailer's product manager has read that streaming 'makes responses faster' and proposes enabling it on the product-description generator to bring the monthly API bill down. Descriptions average around 400 output tokens and the service runs them in bulk overnight, with no user watching. What should the architect tell them?

options.A: Streaming changes when tokens arrive, not how many are generated or billed, so the bill will not move.
options.B: Streaming lowers the bill because a partial response the client cancels mid-generation is not charged.
options.C: Streaming lowers the bill because the incremental wire encoding is more compact than a single response body.
options.D: Streaming lowers the bill because the model generates fewer tokens when it emits them incrementally.

items.question: A freight brokerage extracts shipment manifests as JSON. About one call in thirty returns JSON that fails to parse, and the failures cluster on multi-leg shipments with many line items. The responses that fail all carry a `stop_reason` of `max_tokens`. The current handler catches the parse exception and retries the identical request, which usually fails the same way.

options.A: Add a repair step that closes unbalanced brackets and quotes so the partial manifest parses downstream.
options.B: Instruct the model to summarise each leg more briefly so multi-leg manifests fit inside the existing cap.
options.C: Keep the retry but add exponential backoff and jitter, since one call in thirty failing looks intermittent.
options.D: Branch on the stop reason before parsing, and raise the output cap to cover the largest manifests seen.

items.question: A shared internal AI platform at an energy utility fronts one organisation-level account for eleven product teams. At peak, rate-limit responses spike and every team's latency degrades together; the platform team has no admission control and each team's SDK wrapper retries on its own. Which THREE controls meaningfully protect the shared ceiling? (Choose THREE.)

options.A: A central admission controller that caps in-flight requests and token rate below the account ceiling.
options.B: Raising `max_tokens` on every team's requests so each call returns more content and fewer calls are needed.
options.C: Honouring the retry-after guidance on a rate-limit response instead of reissuing the call immediately.
options.D: Adding an independent retry layer inside each team's SDK wrapper on top of the one in the shared gateway.
options.E: Moving deferrable work such as the nightly backfills off the interactive path onto the Batch API.

items.question: A municipal housing authority summarises case files whose length varies enormously — most are a few pages, a minority run to hundreds. About 2% of submissions fail outright because the assembled request exceeds the model's context window; caseworkers see a generic error after waiting twenty seconds, and there is no signal in advance about which files will fail.

options.A: Count the assembled request's tokens before sending, reserve room for the output, and route oversized files to a chunked path.
options.B: Estimate size by dividing the case file's character count by four and reject any submission above that threshold.
options.C: Catch the context-window error and retry the same assembled request against a higher-capability model tier.
options.D: Truncate every case file to a fixed character length during assembly so no request can overflow the window.

items.question: A media monitoring pipeline asks the model to emit one transcript segment ending with the literal marker `<<<END>>>`, and passes that marker as a stop sequence so generation halts at the segment boundary. A downstream splitter scans the returned text for `<<<END>>>` to find boundaries and now finds none, so every segment is treated as unterminated. Responses come back with `stop_reason` set to `stop_sequence`.

options.A: Stop sequences only match at the start of a line, so the splitter should re-anchor its pattern to line boundaries.
options.B: Stop sequences are advisory, so the pipeline should validate that the model actually emitted the marker and retry when it did not.
options.C: The matched stop sequence is not included in the returned content; the splitter should branch on the stop reason instead.
options.D: The marker was consumed by the SSE decoder as an event delimiter; disabling streaming will restore it to the body.

items.question: A hospital network's patient-messaging assistant drafts replies that nurses review before sending. Policy requires that no draft is displayed until an automated safety and identifier check has passed on the complete text, and separately that generation is aborted the instant an early-warning classifier fires on the text produced so far. Drafts average around 600 tokens. Nurses say the current non-streaming implementation feels dead for several seconds, and the clinical safety lead will not relax either requirement.

options.A: Stream directly to the nurse's client and run the safety and identifier check in the browser, blanking the pane if it fails.
options.B: Keep the call non-streaming and show a progress indicator with an estimated wait, since the display policy rules streaming out.
options.C: Keep the call non-streaming and run the safety and identifier check on the patient record fed into the prompt instead.
options.D: Stream server-side so partial text can be scanned and generation cancelled, releasing to the nurse only after the full-text check passes.

items.question: Which property of a workload is the strongest indicator that the Batch API is the right path for it?

options.A: The prompts share a large invariant prefix that could be reused across many calls.
options.B: The workload is receiving rate-limit responses through the whole of the evening peak.
options.C: The requests are independent and no caller is waiting on any individual result.
options.D: The outputs are long, so delivering them incrementally would improve how the wait feels.

items.question: In a streamed response, where does the caller find the stop reason and the final output-token accounting for the message?

options.A: In the opening event that begins the message, alongside the model identifier and input usage.
options.B: In the message-level delta near the end of the stream, before the message stop event.
options.C: In every content-block delta, each of which carries a running total for the message.
options.D: In an HTTP trailer that the client can read once the connection has been closed.

items.question: A logistics operator is deciding which of its Claude workloads to move onto the Batch API to relieve pressure on its interactive throughput. Which TWO of the following are appropriate candidates? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Classifying inbound customer emails on arrival so a routing decision can be made within a second.
options.B: Re-scoring the entire 400,000-item evaluation corpus after each prompt change, reviewed the following morning.
options.C: A shipment-fraud check embedded in the card payment authorisation path, run before the charge is approved.
options.D: A quarterly re-classification of the seven-year archive of shipping documents ahead of an audit.
options.E: Generating the synchronous reply to an inbound webhook whose sender holds the connection open.

items.question: A software vendor's support agent holds long conversations, commonly running past 30 turns, over a fixed tool set and a large system prompt. The team caches with one breakpoint at the end of the system prompt. Cost and time-to-first-token per turn climb steadily as a conversation proceeds; by turn 30 the great majority of each request's input is transcript that sits after the breakpoint and is reprocessed from scratch every time.

options.A: Advance a breakpoint to the end of the newest completed turn on each request so the transcript caches incrementally.
options.B: Retain more turns in the history so the prefix reaches a stable size sooner and stops changing between requests.
options.C: Move the accumulated transcript into the system prompt so it falls inside the prefix that is already cached each turn.
options.D: Summarise the entire conversation into a single paragraph before every turn so each request stays small.

items.question: An HR software vendor's policy assistant carries a 3,000-token instruction set covering role, tone, refusal rules and output schema. The engineer placed all of it as the first user message rather than in the request's system field, on the basis that 'it works either way'. The product now needs prompt caching to control cost and per-tenant overrides of a handful of the rules. What is the architectural problem with the current placement?

options.A: Instructions carried in a user message are discarded after the first assistant turn, so they must be resent verbatim on every subsequent request.
options.B: The API rejects a request whose opening message contains instructions rather than a question, so the tenant override path will fail at runtime.
options.C: The two placements are functionally interchangeable, so both requirements should be met by reordering the message list rather than by moving anything.
options.D: The instruction set now sits inside the mutable message stream, which makes it harder to hold as a stable cached prefix and to override per tenant.

items.question: An online grocer renders a one-line personalised note on the checkout confirmation page. The call has a hard 400ms server-side budget and the note is explicitly a nice-to-have; a static default exists. During a flash sale the call starts returning rate-limit responses whose retry-after guidance is several seconds. The current handler waits the advised interval and retries, so checkout pages are now stalling for seconds during the busiest hour of the year. What should the team do next?

options.A: Wait the advised interval but cap the wait at the 400ms budget, then retry once inside the same request.
options.B: Treat the rate-limit response as a shed signal: render the static default, record the miss, and do not retry.
options.C: Move note generation to the Batch API overnight and serve the stored result on the customer's next visit.
options.D: Split checkout traffic across more application workers so the notes are generated in parallel during the sale.

items.question: Before sending a request, how should a client obtain an authoritative input token count for the exact system content, messages and tool definitions it is about to submit?

options.A: Call the dedicated token-counting endpoint with exactly the payload the request will carry when it is sent.
options.B: Read the usage figures from the previous response and extrapolate from the change in payload size.
options.C: Divide the total character count of the assembled payload by four and treat that as the count.
options.D: Submit the real request with the output allowance set to zero and read the reported input usage.

items.question: A conveyancing platform is throttled during peak conveyancing hours. The team's first response was to bundle several documents into each request, cutting request count by 70%. Rate-limit responses did not improve at all. The workload is characterised by short prompts producing very long structured outputs — typically a few hundred input tokens and several thousand output tokens per call.

options.A: Bundle further still, since fewer and larger requests always sit more comfortably inside a published limit.
options.B: Add exponential backoff and accept the throttling, since the pressure is transient and will clear as peak passes.
options.C: Split the peak-hour workload across several additional API keys belonging to the same organisation.
options.D: Measure which limit dimension is actually saturating — request rate or token throughput — and target that one.

items.question: A pharmaceutical company submits about 200,000 adverse-event narratives for summarisation through the Batch API each week and loads the results into a safety database that must account for every narrative. Which TWO properties of batch processing must the ingestion design account for? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Each request must carry a caller-supplied identifier, because results are matched by identifier, not by position.
options.B: The batch is committed as an atomic unit, so one malformed narrative invalidates the whole 200,000-item submission.
options.C: Requests succeed or fail independently, so the loader needs a per-request outcome check and a re-drive path.
options.D: Results are pushed to the client incrementally as each request finishes, so the loader must maintain an open receiver.
options.E: Each request inside a batch inherits the interactive endpoint's per-request client timeout and retry policy.

items.question: A marketing agency wants noticeably longer product narratives from its generator. An engineer raises `max_tokens` substantially and redeploys. Output length is unchanged, and responses come back with a stop reason of `end_turn`. Why?

options.A: The account's token throughput ceiling is capping generation before the new allowance can be reached.
options.B: The new allowance only takes effect on streamed requests, and this generator posts non-streaming calls.
options.C: The parameter is a ceiling on what the model may produce, not a target; length is driven by the instruction.
options.D: A configured stop sequence is halting generation first, and it takes precedence over the newly raised allowance.

items.question: A public-sector digital service is hardening the shared client library that all twelve of its delivery teams use to call Claude. Teams currently each write their own error handling, and a recent incident involved retries stacked at three layers. Which THREE of the following belong in the shared library? (Choose THREE.)

options.A: A caller-propagated deadline that bounds the total time spent across the initial attempt and all retries.
options.B: Automatic re-submission of any request that returns a validation error, with the payload re-serialised first.
options.C: Exponential backoff with jitter and a bounded retry budget, owned at this layer and documented as the only retry layer.
options.D: A correlation identifier attached to every request and recorded alongside the response's stop reason and token usage.
options.E: A silent fallback to a lower-capability model tier on every retry, without surfacing it to the caller.

items.question: A news publisher's research assistant produces long briefings and already streams them to the browser through its own backend. Analytics show that around 40% of readers navigate away within the first few seconds, yet the backend generates every briefing to completion regardless, and the monthly output-token spend reflects it. What concrete operational benefit is available here?

options.A: Streaming halts generation automatically when the browser tab closes, so the spend must have another cause.
options.B: The backend can abort the upstream request when the reader disconnects, so the rest is never generated.
options.C: Streamed responses are metered on what the reader actually consumed, so abandoned briefings cost less.
options.D: The model can be told to shorten a briefing mid-generation once analytics signal that the reader has left.

items.question: An engineer at a property portal injects retrieved listing data into the conversation by appending a synthetic assistant message reading 'Here are the listings I found: …' immediately before the buyer's question, so the model treats the data as something it has already said. A reviewer flags it because the stored transcripts are used for quality sampling and for a regulated record of what the assistant told the customer. What is the sound structure?

options.A: Place the retrieved listings as delimited, labelled content inside the user turn that carries the question.
options.B: Keep the synthetic assistant turn but annotate it in the system field as machine-inserted rather than model-generated.
options.C: Move the retrieved listings into the system field on every request so that they always precede the question.
options.D: Append the listings to the buyer's earlier user message from a previous turn so the history stays compact.

items.question: A claims intake flow makes three dependent Claude calls in sequence — extract, then validate, then summarise — behind a synchronous API whose published contract promises a response within 18 seconds. Each call's HTTP client was configured independently with a 10-second timeout and one retry. In production the endpoint frequently returns after 25 to 30 seconds and breaches the contract, even though no individual call ever times out.

options.A: Reduce each call's timeout to six seconds so that three sequential calls fit inside the eighteen-second contract.
options.B: Issue the three calls in parallel so end-to-end latency is bounded by the slowest of them rather than by their sum.
options.C: Propagate one end-to-end deadline so each hop gets only the time remaining, and skip a hop that cannot fit.
options.D: Renegotiate the published contract to forty-five seconds so the observed end-to-end distribution fits inside it.

items.question: A marketplace classifies seller reviews for policy violations at roughly 4 million reviews a month, all processed on a nightly schedule with no user waiting. Each request is a 250-token instruction block and schema followed by the review text, which averages 900 tokens and is unique to each request. Outputs are a short structured verdict. An engineer proposes enabling prompt caching on the instruction block as the main cost initiative for the quarter.

options.A: Enable it and add a second breakpoint after the review text so the whole request is covered by the cache.
options.B: Reverse the order so the review text leads and the instruction block follows, improving locality for the cache.
options.C: Skip caching and raise the output allowance instead so each of the 4 million classifications completes in one call.
options.D: Enable caching, but note that only a fifth of each request is reusable; the bigger levers are tier and batch.

items.question: Which TWO stop reasons tell the caller that the assistant's turn is not yet complete, so returning the content as a final answer would be wrong? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: `max_tokens`, because generation was cut off when the output ceiling was reached.
options.B: `end_turn`, because the model has produced the whole reply it intended to produce.
options.C: `tool_use`, because the model has paused and needs a tool result before it can carry on.
options.D: `stop_sequence`, because a marker that the caller configured in the request was matched.
options.E: A rate-limit response arriving in place of a completed message during peak load.

items.question: A wealth-management firm's advisory assistant carries a 25,000-token system prompt of product rules and disclosure language. Prompt caching was enabled and delivered a substantial reduction in cost and time-to-first-token for two weeks. After the most recent release the hit rate went to zero and both metrics reverted. The release note lists one change to the prompt: a line added at the very top reading `Current date and time: {{now}}`, rendered to the second, so compliance could evidence that the model was told the date. What should the team do next?

options.A: Move the timestamp out of the cached prefix and into the per-request user turn that follows the breakpoint.
options.B: Remove the timestamp line entirely and rely on the model's own sense of today's date for disclosures.
options.C: Move the cache breakpoint to sit immediately after the timestamp line so the timestamp is cached too.
options.D: Synchronise clocks across the fleet so every instance renders the identical second and prefixes match.

items.question: An engineer at a travel platform streams a response whose content is a single large JSON itinerary. To show progress, the UI attempts to parse the accumulated buffer after every delta and renders whatever parses successfully. Most attempts throw and are swallowed, but occasionally a partially-arrived structure parses cleanly and the UI renders an itinerary that is missing its later legs. One customer has already booked from such a render.

options.A: Increase the client's delta buffer size so each parse attempt runs on a larger slice of the itinerary.
options.B: Accumulate deltas without parsing, parse once the block's terminating event arrives, and drive progress from delta arrival.
options.C: Ask the model to emit the itinerary's fields in reverse dependency order so each early fragment is self-contained and renderable.
options.D: Abandon streaming on this endpoint, since a large structured itinerary cannot be delivered incrementally.

items.question: A government benefits portal added streaming to its eligibility explainer so applicants see text appear rather than staring at a spinner. Against the origin service, tokens arrive incrementally exactly as expected. Through the public URL, applicants still see nothing for eight seconds and then the whole explanation at once. The path from the browser to the origin runs through a CDN and a reverse proxy.

options.A: Shorten the explanation so the intermediary's buffer fills and flushes more often during generation.
options.B: Configure the CDN and reverse proxy to pass event streams through unbuffered, and verify from the browser.
options.C: Move the explainer to WebSockets, since HTTP intermediaries cannot forward an incrementally generated response.
options.D: Ask the model for shorter sentences so the origin emits smaller, more frequent events over the stream.

items.question: An education publisher generates full curriculum guides — thirty to forty pages of structured material — from a syllabus in a single call. The team has already set the output allowance to the highest value the model accepts, and the longer syllabi still return with a `max_tokens` stop reason. They have tried three models in the same family and see the same behaviour on the same inputs.

options.A: Enable streaming, which lifts the per-response output limit because tokens are delivered as produced, not in one body.
options.B: Retry the truncated requests, since generated length varies between samples and an attempt will eventually fit.
options.C: Decompose the guide into sections generated by separate calls against a shared plan, and assemble the results client-side.
options.D: Set the output allowance above the model's ceiling and log the resulting validation error as a warning to ignore.

items.question: In a retry policy, what does randomised jitter provide that exponential backoff on its own does not?

options.A: It shortens the total time spent retrying, because some of the waits come out randomly shorter.
options.B: It guarantees that a retry never fires before the server's advised retry-after interval has fully elapsed.
options.C: It bounds the number of attempts a client may make, so retries cannot continue indefinitely.
options.D: It decorrelates retry timing across clients, so a fleet that failed together does not retry in unison.

items.question: A contact-centre assistant replays the full conversation on every turn and finishes each escalation with a written summary for the case record. To keep long escalations from being rejected, the client computes the output allowance as the context window minus the current input size. Most conversations are fine, but on long escalations — exactly the ones the case record matters most for — summaries come back visibly clipped with a `max_tokens` stop reason.

options.A: Reserve an output budget sized from what the summaries need, and trim older turns to fit the input into what remains.
options.B: Drop the dynamic calculation and set the allowance to the largest value the model accepts on every request.
options.C: Start a fresh conversation once an escalation passes a 40-turn threshold, so the replayed history never grows large.
options.D: Accept the clipping and add a second call that expands the clipped summary into a complete case record.

items.question: A public-records search assistant sends a 30,000-token invariant reference corpus plus a short user query on every call. Its p95 time before the first token reaches the user is 6.5 seconds, against an internal target of 2 seconds. Answers are short. Which THREE changes address that metric? (Choose THREE.)

options.A: Cache the invariant corpus behind a breakpoint so it is not reprocessed from scratch on every request.
options.B: Raise the output allowance so the model is never constrained while producing an answer to a records query.
options.C: Stream the response so the first token reaches the user as produced, not after the answer is finished.
options.D: Group several users' queries into a single request so the 30,000-token corpus is amortised across them.
options.E: Move rarely-consulted portions of the corpus out of the standard request and load them only when needed.

items.question: A retail media platform currently discovers it is near its throughput ceiling only when requests start being rejected. The platform team wants to shape traffic before rejections begin. They have been explicit that they will not hard-code any figure that could change when the account's limits are revised, because a stale constant caused a previous incident.

options.A: Sample the rejection rate over a rolling window and reduce client concurrency once it crosses a threshold.
options.B: Configure a fixed requests-per-second cap in the gateway, derived from last quarter's observed peak traffic level.
options.C: Drive admission control from the remaining allowance and reset time reported in the rate-limit response headers.
options.D: Route overflow requests through a second organisation account so the primary account's allowance can recover.

items.question: What effect does enabling prompt caching have on the content of the model's response?

options.A: A previously produced response is returned verbatim whenever the same prompt is seen again.
options.B: None: caching changes how the prefix is processed and billed, not what the model produces for a request.
options.C: Responses become more consistent, because the cached prefix also fixes the sampling behaviour.
options.D: Responses become shorter, because content covered by the cache does not need to be restated.

items.question: A team is adding idempotency to a pipeline in which a Claude call is followed by a write to a customer record. Which TWO statements are correct? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Setting sampling temperature to zero makes a retried generation return identical content, enough to deduplicate the write.
options.B: The guarantee must be enforced at the mutating step, keyed by a caller-supplied value that stays stable across retries.
options.C: Idempotency becomes unnecessary once the client's own retry logic is removed from the pipeline entirely.
options.D: A retried generation call may return different content, so deduplication cannot be based on comparing outputs.
options.E: The idempotency key should be derived by hashing the model's response, so identical outputs collapse into a single write.

items.question: A live-sports product generates one-line commentary updates with a hard 900ms budget from event to display; a late line is discarded rather than shown. Median latency is 300ms but p99 is 2.4 seconds, and the tail is what viewers notice. The call is read-only and has no side effects. The team proposes issuing a second identical request whenever the first has not returned within 350ms.

options.A: Lower the client timeout to 350ms with a single retry, which achieves the same tail reduction far more simply.
options.B: Hedge every request from the outset so the faster of the two always wins, treating the extra spend as the price of the latency target.
options.C: Reject hedging outright: duplicating requests under a 900ms budget can only add load and lengthen the tail.
options.D: Adopt threshold hedging, cancel the loser when one returns, cap the hedged share of traffic, and confirm there are no side effects.

items.question: A telehealth triage assistant persists conversation state so patients can resume a session and clinicians can review what was exchanged. The implementation stores the fully rendered request that was sent to the API — system content, entire replayed history and all — as one blob per turn. Six months in, the team cannot say which prompt version produced a given reply, cannot replay a conversation under a revised prompt, and the store is growing quadratically because every turn re-persists the whole history.

options.A: Persist each structured turn once with the prompt and model version identifiers, and render the request at call time.
options.B: Continue storing rendered requests, but compress each blob and shorten the retention period to 90 days.
options.C: Store only the final assistant reply for each turn, since that is what clinicians actually review afterwards.
options.D: Store a hash of the rendered request alongside each reply so that prompt changes can at least be detected after the fact.

items.question: A SaaS vendor serving 900 corporate customers wants to cache a 12,000-token instruction and schema block that is byte-identical for every customer. Each request also carries customer-specific documents. The security review has blocked the change on the grounds that a shared cache means one customer's data could be served to another. The engineering lead needs a resolution that satisfies the reviewer without giving up the saving.

options.A: Give each of the 900 customers its own cached prefix by appending their customer identifier to the instruction block.
options.B: Accept the objection and rule prompt caching out for any workload that serves more than one corporate tenant.
options.C: Keep the invariant instruction and schema in the shared prefix and place customer documents after the breakpoint.
options.D: Encrypt the customer documents before including them so no readable customer data can ever enter the cache.

items.question: Setting aside how the wait feels to a user, why is streaming operationally useful for a single long-running generation?

options.A: It gives the client continuous evidence of progress, so a stall can be told apart from slow generation.
options.B: It reduces the total number of tokens the model must generate to satisfy the same long instruction.
options.C: It removes the response from the account's throughput accounting for the period the stream is open.
options.D: It lets a single response exceed the model's output ceiling by delivering the remainder in later events.

items.question: A retail analytics team submits a 90,000-request batch each night. Last night the submission call failed with a network error after the request body had been sent, so the client has no confirmation of whether the batch was registered. The on-call operator must act before the morning deadline. A duplicate batch would double the night's spend and produce two result sets the loader cannot tell apart. What should the operator do next?

options.A: Resubmit immediately, since a duplicate batch is cheaper than missing the deadline; delete the surplus afterwards.
options.B: Query the batch service for a job matching the submission's caller-supplied identifier, and submit only if none is found.
options.C: Wait for the usual turnaround window to elapse and resubmit only if no results have appeared by then.
options.D: Resubmit under a new identifier and reconcile the two result sets against the source records in the morning.
